(CNN) -- From cyberspace to college campuses, many young conservatives are worried that Sen. John McCain is not appealing to their generation. Sen. John McCain says he knows how important young voters are. At a town hall meeting in Ohio this month, a student told McCain that Republicans were a dying breed on his campus. "I understand the challenge I have, and I understand that this election is really all about the people of your generation," McCain said. Many young Republicans said Sen. Barack Obama, the 46-year-old junior senator from Illinois, is inspiring voters their age, but McCain, the 71-year-old Arizona senator who has been in office since the early '80s, is not. Eric Perlmutter, a Republican and student at the at the University of Southern California, said the roaring enthusiasm that follows Obama is missing among conservatives his age. "We try to get people out to our college Republican meetings, but ... we can't seem to draw the same kind of vocal support," he said. At the July town hall meeting in Portsmouth, Ohio, McCain said he knows that he has "a lot of work to do" with the younger voters. The senator said he needs young conservatives to help spread his message for him, because "there's nothing that convinces young people like other young people." McCain also acknowledged the importance of using the Internet to reach out to a generation that stays in touch via social networking sites. On MySpace, Obama has more than 427,000 friends, compared with fewer than 60,000 for McCain. Perlmutter said he cringed when McCain admitted he doesn't use e-mail. Obama, however, is frequently seen with Blackberry in hand. Additionally, Perlmutter pointed out that the images used in McCain's campaign -- such as a message about small businesses showing a barber shop with a traditional red and blue pole -- hardly connect to the younger generation. "Well, when you see the Main Street barber shop image, you think of 1950s America. An entrepreneur, a Silicon Valley guy would definitely make him more attractive," he said. Obama also has increased his college-age appeal by holding rallies and giving speeches at hundreds of campuses. McCain has said he recognizes that he needs to get out to those venues "where young people are engaged and receiving their information and forming their opinions." "Sen. McCain should demand that these same colleges and universities host him or else their tax-exempt status could be in jeopardy," said Jason Mattera, spokesman for Young America's Foundation, a conservative outreach group. McCain must work to connect young voters to conservative principles, Mattera said. "So if they are suspicious of Uncle Sam telling them what Internet sites they can view, they should be equally suspicious of the federal government telling them what health care plan they are going to be a part of," he said. According to a Pew Research Center study conducted between October and March, McCain has a big numbers gap to close. The study found that the current generation of young voters, those who came of age during the President Bush years, are giving the Democrats a wide edge. Fifty-eight percent of voters under 30 identified or leaned toward the Democratic Party, compared with 33 percent who said they identified or leaned toward the Republican Party. The McCain campaign said it plans to increase the senator's presence on sites such as Facebook and MySpace in addition to the candidate making appearance on shows that appeal to younger viewers, such as "The Daily Show with Jon Stewart," "The Tonight Show with Jay Leno" and the "Late Show with David Letterman." In past elections, both parties have tended to put less focus on younger voters because historically, their turnout has been low. With fewer than four months until the November election, McCain said he's confident he can convince young voters that he is the candidate for them. "I believe that I can convince them that I have the plan of action and the ideals and the goals and the inspiration that, as next president of the United States, I can serve better their interests than my opponent," he said.

In past elections, both parties have tended to place less emphasis on younger voters because their turnout has historically been low.

With fewer than four months remaining before the November election, McCain said he is confident he can convince young voters that he is the right candidate for them.

“I believe that I can convince them that I have the plan of action and the ideals and the goals and the inspiration that, as next president of the United States, I can serve better their interests than my opponent,” he said.

counterfactuals.output:
**McCain faces youth gap as Obama dominates campuses and the social Web**

*October 2008 — Washington*

As Sen. John McCain makes his final push for the White House, the Republican nominee is confronting a problem that goes beyond swing states and daily tracking polls: a noticeable struggle to connect with younger voters, including many young conservatives who say they admire his service but are not energized by his campaign.

On college campuses, Sen. Barack Obama’s operation has become a defining feature of the 2008 race. Student volunteers wearing Obama buttons can be found registering voters, organizing debate-watch parties and using Facebook, text messages and e-mail lists to turn political enthusiasm into turnout. McCain, meanwhile, has leaned on a more traditional campaign model — town halls, veterans’ events and appeals to experience — that has not generated the same level of youth excitement.

The contrast is especially visible online. Obama’s campaign has built a massive digital presence, using social networking sites and online fundraising to mobilize supporters. Young voters are sharing videos, joining Facebook groups and forwarding campaign messages at a pace Republicans have struggled to match.

McCain’s advisers argue that enthusiasm on campuses does not necessarily translate into votes, and they say the Arizona senator’s message on national security, fiscal restraint and reform still appeals to younger conservatives. But some Republican students say the campaign has had difficulty speaking their language.

“I respect Senator McCain, especially because of his military service,” said one College Republican at a battleground-state university. “But Obama’s campaign feels like it’s everywhere. They’re on our phones, on Facebook, in our dorms. McCain’s campaign feels more like something our parents are watching on TV.”

McCain has tried to counter the enthusiasm gap in part through his running mate, Alaska Gov. Sarah Palin, who has drawn large crowds and strong support from the party’s conservative base. Palin’s rallies have energized many Republicans who had been lukewarm toward McCain, particularly evangelical voters and social conservatives.

But among younger voters, the Palin pick has produced mixed results. Some young conservatives say she brings excitement and a populist edge to the ticket. Others say the campaign’s emphasis on culture-war themes has done little to address issues that younger voters cite as priorities, including college costs, jobs, energy policy and the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Obama, 47, has benefited from a broader generational appeal. His campaign has framed his candidacy as a break from the politics of the past, a message that resonates with students who were in grade school during the Clinton impeachment fight and came of age during the September 11 attacks and the Iraq war. His opposition to the Iraq war from the beginning has also helped him with younger voters, many of whom see foreign policy as a defining issue.

McCain, 72, has sought to make his age and experience an asset, repeatedly arguing that he is tested and prepared to lead in a dangerous world. He has also emphasized his record as a political maverick, pointing to past clashes with his own party over campaign finance, immigration and government spending.

Yet that message has been complicated by the political environment. President George W. Bush remains deeply unpopular, and Democrats have worked to tie McCain to the outgoing administration. For younger voters who associate the Republican Party with the Iraq war and the economic downturn, McCain’s promise of reform has often been a tough sell.

Polls throughout the campaign have shown Obama with a commanding lead among voters under 30. The question for Republicans is whether McCain can limit the damage by motivating young conservatives and independents who might be skeptical of Obama but uninspired by the GOP ticket.

Republican strategists acknowledge that the party faces a long-term challenge if it cannot compete more effectively for younger voters. The 2008 campaign, they say, has exposed a gap not only in message but in technology and organization.

“Obama is not just winning young voters with speeches,” said one Republican consultant. “He’s meeting them where they live — online, on campus, in social networks. Republicans have to learn from that.”

For McCain, the immediate task is narrower: hold together the Republican coalition, win over undecided independents and hope that Obama’s youth advantage does not translate into overwhelming turnout on Election Day.

But on many campuses, the energy gap is hard to miss. Obama volunteers are knocking on dorm-room doors and sending reminders through Facebook. McCain supporters are working, too — but often with fewer people, fewer resources and less visible momentum.

In a campaign defined by change, McCain is betting that experience will still matter most. Among young voters, however, Obama has turned the race into something that looks less like a campaign and more like a movement — and McCain is still trying to catch up.

**Young Republicans Weigh McCain’s Challenge With Youth Vote**

*By [Reporter Name]*

As Sen. John McCain campaigns for the presidency, some young Republicans say they admire his military service, independence and experience — but worry that his campaign is struggling to connect with voters their age in a race increasingly shaped by youth enthusiasm and online organizing.

McCain, the Arizona Republican and presumptive GOP nominee, would be 72 years old shortly after taking office if elected. His age has become a recurring subject among younger voters, particularly as he faces Sen. Barack Obama, whose campaign has drawn large crowds of college students and young professionals and built a reputation for energetic outreach through the internet and social networking sites.

Adding to the contrast, McCain has acknowledged that he does not regularly use e-mail, a detail critics have seized on as evidence that he is out of step with a generation accustomed to instant messaging, Facebook, MySpace and text-message organizing. Supporters argue that the focus on technology is unfair and that McCain’s record on national security, government spending and political reform matters more than whether he personally sends e-mails.

Still, young Republicans say the perception gap is real.

“Senator McCain has a compelling story, but the campaign has to tell it in a way that reaches people where they are,” said one college Republican activist. “For voters under 30, that means online — not just speeches and television ads.”

Obama’s campaign has made youth outreach a central part of its strategy, using Facebook, MySpace, YouTube and campaign-built social networking tools to recruit volunteers, raise money and turn supporters into organizers. His events on college campuses have often drawn thousands, reinforcing the image of a campaign powered by younger voters.

McCain’s campaign has also used social media platforms, including MySpace and Facebook, and Republican student groups have worked to promote his candidacy online. But many young GOP activists concede that Democrats appear to have an advantage in enthusiasm and digital organizing.

Polling data has underscored the challenge. Surveys throughout the campaign have shown Democrats leading Republicans among voters under 30, with Obama holding a particularly strong advantage over McCain in that age group. The numbers reflect a broader generational shift that has concerned Republican strategists: younger voters are more likely than older voters to identify with or lean toward the Democratic Party.

For McCain, the task is twofold — reassuring older and more traditional Republican voters while also finding a message that resonates with younger Americans worried about the Iraq war, the economy, college affordability and the country’s direction.

Young Republicans say McCain still has openings. Some point to his reputation as a political maverick, his support for national service and his willingness to break with his party on issues such as campaign finance and climate change. Others say his biography as a Vietnam prisoner of war gives him credibility that transcends age.

But they also say biography alone may not be enough.

“Young voters want authenticity, but they also want accessibility,” said another Republican student organizer. “If the campaign doesn’t compete aggressively online, it risks letting Obama define the race for an entire generation.”

With Democrats showing strength among voters under 30, McCain’s campaign faces pressure to modernize its outreach and sharpen its appeal to young Americans. Whether young Republicans can help bridge that gap may be a key test of the GOP’s ability to compete beyond its traditional base.

**McCain Faces Youth Gap as Obama Turns Campuses and the Web Into Campaign Weapons**

*By Staff Writer*

As the 2008 presidential campaign moves from primaries to the general election, Senator John McCain faces a challenge that is not only ideological or partisan, but generational.

On college campuses, in online organizing networks and across social media sites, Senator Barack Obama has built a visible advantage among younger voters — a bloc that has historically been unreliable at the polls but could prove decisive if enthusiasm translates into turnout.

Obama’s campaign has made youth outreach central to its strategy, blending traditional campus organizing with a sophisticated Internet operation. His supporters have used Facebook groups, MySpace pages, YouTube videos, text messaging and the campaign’s own social network, My.BarackObama.com, to recruit volunteers, raise money and organize events.

McCain, by contrast, has struggled to match Obama’s online intensity and campus presence. While the Arizona senator has support from young conservatives and Republican student groups, his candidacy has often been defined by his decades of experience, military service and seniority — strengths among older voters, but less naturally appealing to a generation raised on digital politics.

The divide is reflected in polling. Surveys by the Pew Research Center during the campaign have shown Obama with a substantial advantage among voters under 30. Pew has also found younger Americans to be more Democratic-leaning than older voters, more skeptical of the Iraq war and more comfortable using the Internet as a political tool. In Pew’s analysis, the so-called Millennial generation has shown signs of becoming one of the most Democratic age cohorts in modern politics.

That trend poses a direct problem for McCain. Although he has long cultivated an image as a maverick and has appealed to independents in past races, many younger voters associate him with Republican President George W. Bush, the Iraq war and an older style of politics. Obama, meanwhile, has framed his campaign around change, technology and generational transition.

On campuses, the contrast is often unmistakable. Obama tables and rallies have drawn large crowds at universities across the country, with students signing up online to volunteer or travel to battleground states. His campaign has encouraged peer-to-peer organizing, allowing students to create events, raise money and contact voters through digital tools.

McCain’s student supporters say the race on campus is not as one-sided as it appears. Organizations such as College Republicans, Young America’s Foundation and Students for McCain have worked to promote the Republican nominee, arguing that Obama’s popularity among students masks weaknesses on taxes, national security and experience.

Conservative youth organizers also point to McCain’s biography — his years as a prisoner of war, his record on government spending and his willingness to break with his party — as qualities that can appeal to young voters who value authenticity. But they acknowledge that the Republican Party faces a difficult climate after eight years in the White House and widespread discontent over the war and the economy.

The online numbers have reinforced the perception of an enthusiasm gap. Obama has attracted far more followers and friends on major social networking platforms than McCain, while his campaign has dominated viral video sharing and small-dollar online fundraising. Pro-Obama videos have drawn millions of views, and the campaign’s email and text-message lists have become central tools for mobilization.

McCain’s campaign has expanded its Internet operation, but it has not matched Obama’s scale. The difference is not simply technological; it reflects a broader cultural gap. Obama’s supporters often treat online organizing as a natural extension of political identity, while McCain’s campaign has relied more heavily on television, earned media and traditional Republican networks.

Pew Research Center findings have underscored why that matters. Younger voters are far more likely than older Americans to use social networking sites and to get campaign information online. They are also more likely to share political content, watch candidate videos and participate in politics through digital platforms. For campaigns, that means the Internet is not just a fundraising device — it is where many young voters encounter politics in the first place.

Still, Democrats face a familiar warning: youth enthusiasm does not always equal Election Day turnout. Young voters have historically participated at lower rates than older Americans. Obama’s challenge is to convert campus excitement and online support into actual ballots, especially in swing states with large student populations.

Republicans hope that McCain can narrow the gap by emphasizing experience, national security and bipartisan credentials. They also believe some young voters may reconsider Obama as the campaign intensifies and scrutiny grows.

But for now, the generational contrast remains one of the defining features of the race. McCain is asking voters to trust a veteran legislator with a long record of service. Obama is asking them to join a movement powered by youth, networks and the promise of change.

On America’s college campuses, that message has given Obama a clear head start. For McCain, closing the gap may require more than a better website or more Facebook friends. It may require convincing a generation eager to turn the page that experience can be its own form of change.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a 2008 election article in the style of CNN analyzing why many young conservatives are not enthusiastic about John McCain and what his campaign plans to do to improve his appeal among younger voters.
counterfactuals.output:
**Young conservatives wary of McCain as campaign looks to close enthusiasm gap**

*By [Staff Writer]*  
*WASHINGTON (2008)*

Sen. John McCain has spent much of his political career cultivating an image as a maverick — a Republican willing to challenge his own party on issues from campaign finance reform to immigration. But as the Arizona senator moves toward the general election, that reputation is creating a problem with a group Republicans will need in November: young conservatives.

While McCain has secured the Republican nomination, he has not yet generated the kind of excitement among younger voters that Democrats Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton have drawn on campuses and online. For many young conservatives, McCain is respected as a war hero and experienced public servant, but not necessarily embraced as the future of the Republican Party.

The concern inside GOP circles is not that young conservatives will vote Democratic in large numbers. The bigger worry is that they may not volunteer, donate, organize or turn out at the levels needed in a close election.

### A generational enthusiasm gap

McCain’s challenge begins with style as much as ideology.

Obama, in particular, has built a campaign that speaks the language of younger voters — heavy on social networking, text messaging, online fundraising and large rally events. McCain, by contrast, has often appeared more comfortable in town halls than on YouTube, and his campaign has not matched the Democratic operation’s early digital energy.

But the tension also runs deeper.

Some young conservatives remain skeptical of McCain because of positions he has taken over the years that put him at odds with the Republican base. His support for a bipartisan immigration overhaul angered many conservatives who viewed it as amnesty. His signature campaign finance legislation, co-written with Democratic Sen. Russ Feingold, has long been criticized by conservative activists. His past opposition to some tax cuts under President Bush also left lingering doubts among fiscal conservatives.

To many young Republicans who came of age during the Bush years and through conservative media, McCain’s independence is not always seen as strength. For some, it is a reminder that he has often been a thorn in the side of his own party.

### Respect, but limited passion

Interviews with young GOP activists suggest a common theme: admiration without excitement.

McCain’s military service and years as a prisoner of war in Vietnam give him a personal story few candidates can match. His supporters say that biography should resonate with young voters looking for authenticity and sacrifice in public life.

But younger conservatives who are motivated by limited government, judicial appointments, gun rights, national security and cultural issues often say they want clearer signals that McCain will govern as a reliable conservative.

His campaign has tried to reassure them by emphasizing his support for lower taxes, spending restraint, the Second Amendment, a strong military and conservative judges. Still, doubts remain among voters who remember McCain’s clashes with evangelical leaders and conservative activists during his 2000 presidential campaign.

### Campaign looks to sharpen message

McCain advisers know they cannot afford to cede the youth vote entirely to Democrats, even if younger voters typically lean less Republican than older voters. The campaign’s goal is to narrow the gap, energize young conservatives and appeal to independents who admire McCain’s reputation for bipartisanship.

To do that, the campaign is expected to focus on several areas:

**National security:** McCain plans to make his experience on military and foreign policy central to his pitch. Advisers believe younger conservatives remain strongly interested in the war on terror, Iraq and America’s role in the world. McCain’s support for the troop surge in Iraq, once politically risky, is now being presented as evidence of judgment and resolve.

**Fiscal discipline:** The campaign is likely to emphasize McCain’s long record opposing earmarks and wasteful spending. For young voters worried about debt, entitlement costs and the size of government, McCain will argue that he has credibility as a budget hawk.

**Judges and social issues:** McCain will continue to highlight his pledge to appoint strict constructionist judges, a key issue for conservatives concerned about the Supreme Court and federal courts. His campaign also points to his anti-abortion record as evidence that he is aligned with social conservatives, despite past tensions with some religious leaders.

**Technology and outreach:** McCain’s team is working to improve its online presence, recognizing that Democrats have had a major head start in digital organizing. Expect more web videos, targeted e-mails, youth-oriented coalitions and efforts to recruit college Republicans as visible campaign surrogates.

**Straight-talk image:** Rather than trying to mimic Obama’s style, McCain is expected to lean into his own brand — town halls, unscripted exchanges and direct appeals to voters tired of partisan politics. His aides believe that authenticity could help with younger voters who are skeptical of traditional political messaging.

### The Obama factor

McCain’s problem is sharpened by Obama’s appeal. The Illinois senator has become a cultural and political phenomenon among younger voters, drawing massive crowds and using online networks to convert enthusiasm into money and volunteers.

That creates a difficult contrast for Republicans. McCain, 71, is running on experience and tested leadership. Obama, 46, is running on change and generational transition. Among young voters, the Democratic message has obvious advantages in tone and energy.

Still, McCain’s advisers argue the election will not be decided by excitement alone. They believe that as voters focus on national security, taxes and commander-in-chief qualifications, McCain can win over young independents and bring skeptical young conservatives home.

### A test for the GOP

The broader question is whether McCain can help Republicans rebuild their connection to younger Americans at a time when the party’s brand has been damaged by the Iraq war, the economy and President Bush’s low approval ratings.

For young conservatives, the choice may come down to whether McCain can convince them that his independence is not a rejection of conservative principles, but a way to make those principles more credible to the wider electorate.

The campaign has time to make that case. But enthusiasm cannot be manufactured overnight.

If McCain hopes to compete with the Democratic nominee in the fall, he will need young conservatives to do more than respect him. He will need them to show up.
